L212: 
L213: The cite95†Lord Howe Island Marine Park†www.dpi.nsw.gov.au (LHIMP) occurs in NSW State waters surrounding Lord Howe Island and Balls Pyramid and is internationally significant, with the world's southern-most true coral reef and the only fringing coral reef lagoon in NSW. The convergence of the warm and cool ocean currents creates an extraordinary mix of colourful tropical and temperate marine life.
L214: The park is home to more than 500 species of fish, over 90 species of coral, turtles, sharks, dolphins and countless other marine creatures, many of which are only found in the region.
L215: ### Importance to the Island
L216: 
L217: The marine park is of social, cultural and economic importance to the island and tourists from around the world visit the marine park to swim, snorkel, dive, fish, kayak, explore and holiday. Commercial activities include charter fishing, scuba diving, snorkelling, sightseeing cruises and beach activities.
L218: ### Park management
L219: 
L220: The management plan for the LHIMP protects marine biodiversity and areas of social and economic importance, and provides for ecologically sustainable use and public enjoyment of this World Heritage listed marine park. The cite96†Zoning Map†www.dpi.nsw.gov.au and cite97†User Guide†www.dpi.nsw.gov.au provide information about the zoning arrangements and management rules in the park.
L221: ### Commonwealth waters
L222: 
L223: The cite98†Lord Howe Marine Park†parksaustralia.gov.au (Commonwealth waters) extends beyond the 3 nautical mile limit of the State water park and covers 110,126 square kilometres. This marine park includes Elizabeth Reef and Middleton Reef which are unique areas home to the rare and gentle black rockcod and green turtle amongst other protected species.

L25: ## Summary
L26: 
L27: The Ningaloo Coast, located on the remote western coast of Australia, is an astonishing place. The dramatic land and seascapes of the region tells unparalleled stories across time, latitude and species, about the movement of continents, changing climates and the evolution of life over 150 million years.
L28: 
L29: ## Image gallery
L30: 
L31: Click an image for a larger view.
L32: 
L33:   * cite3†More images from the Australian Heritage Photographic Library†www.environment.gov.au L34: ## Life beneath the sea
L35: The waters of the Ningaloo Coast contain one of the best developed near-shore reefs in the world, a continuous series of more than 200 kilometres of spectacular wave-swept ramparts off a rugged limestone peninsula, including spectacular coral and sponge gardens and the world famous whale shark.
L36: The history of tropical marine environments during the last few million years is chronicled in the limestone parapets and wave-cut terraces of Cape Range, which record previous high water levels, earlier reefs and the emergence of the peninsula as an island from beneath the sea.
L37: ## Life beneath the land
L38: Below the sunbaked surface of Cape Range lies a hidden network of caves, groundwater streams, pools and aquifers, which house remarkable subterranean fauna. These underground animals, which live only in the Cape Range peninsula aquifer, were separated from their free-floating marine ancestors over 150 million years ago as the supercontinent Pangaea broke apart and the world began to take on the geography we see today.
L39: The only living relatives of these animals are scattered around the world, restricted to a few communities in the North Atlantic Ocean, Caribbean and Mediterranean Seas.
L40: ## Indigenous significance
L41: Archaeological deposits in the rock shelters on Cape Range show Aboriginal peoples' sophisticated knowledge of marine resources between 35,000 and 17,000 years ago. Shell beads discovered at Cape Range have been dated to more than 32,000 old, which is the earliest evidence known in Australia for the manufacture of personal ornaments. Given that only a handful of the caves and rock shelters of this region have been explored, the Ningaloo Coast has great potential to reveal more hidden cultural treasures.
L42: ## National Heritage List
L43: Due to its extraordinary natural qualities and Indigenous significance, the Ningaloo Coast is considered to have outstanding heritage value to the nation and has been included in the Australian National Heritage List. Places listed in the National Heritage List are protected under the Commonwealth Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999.
L44: The EPBC (Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation) Act requires that approval be obtained before any action takes place that could have a significant impact on the national heritage values of a listed place.
L45: ## Consultation with Indigenous people about the Ningaloo Coast national heritage listed place
L46: 
L47: The Indigenous values of the Ningaloo Coast National Heritage Place are not definitively mapped. Indigenous people are the primary source of information on the value of their heritage and should be consulted on a proposed action likely to significantly impact on the listed Indigenous heritage values of the place and/or on a protected matter that has Indigenous heritage values (like listed threatened species).
L48: Prior to undertaking any action, proponents should contact the appropriate Aboriginal Traditional Owners and custodians of the land on which the action will occur that has listed values that may be significantly impacted, as well as the Aboriginal Traditional Owners and custodians of adjoining lands that may be significantly impacted by the action.
L49: A letter from the appropriate representative bodies declaring that they have been adequately consulted on the action informs the Department that a best practice approach has been undertaken. Further information on Aboriginal representative bodies is available from cite4†Native Title Corporations†www.nativetitle.org.au or via local Aboriginal Land Councils.
L50: Guidance about best practice Indigenous engagement can be found at cite5†Engage early – guidance for proponents on best practice Indigenous engagement for environmental assessments under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999 (EPBC (Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation) Act) .

L169: # Coral Sea Marine Park
L170: 
L171: South Islet (Willis Islets), Bird Islet (Wreck Reef), North East Cay (the Herald Cays) and Magdelaine Cay South are about 500 km off Queensland’s east coast. These areas are now closed to the public to cite118†protect and restore these locations .
L172: 
L173: Welcome to the Coral Sea Marine Park, one of Australia’s most spectacular marine treasures.
L174: The park covers 989,836 square kilometres and has a depth range from 0-6,000m, lies off the coast of Queensland beyond the Great Barrier Reef, and is one of the world’s largest marine parks.
L175: 
L176: The Coral Sea Marine Park (CSMP) has a diverse array of habitats, such as coral reefs, islands, sandy cays, deep sea plains and canyons.
L177: 
L178: Far beyond the Great Barrier Reef, this marine park protects:
L179:   * 16 different seafloor environments (including seamounts, canyons and plains)
L180:   * 34 vast reef areas and 67 cays and islets
L181:   * 15,000 km² of reef systems
L182:   * an abundance of marine life.
L183: 
L184: Here you can find unspoiled world-class dive sites, such as isolated reefs, where colourful coral walls are the perfect backdrop for cruising reef sharks.
L185: 
L186: The park includes iconic black marlin spawning aggregations near Osprey Reef, and every year humpback whales migrate through the marine park from Antarctica.
L187: You might catch a glimpse of a delicately patterned pipefish, or spot a huge, boldly blotched potato cod. Either way, the excellent visibility will help. You can expect to see for up to 60 metres.
L188: 
L189: Above the water, marine turtles and seabirds breed in safety on isolated cays. Six of the world’s seven species of marine turtles can be found in the Coral Sea.
L190: 
L191: This marine park is enormous (2200 km at its longest and 1300 km at its widest).
L192: The Coral Sea Marine Park is managed using National Park, Habitat Protection and Special Purpose zones.
L193: 
L194: Parks Australia in collaboration with universities, state government agencies and federal partners is conducting research to inform monitoring and ongoing management of the Coral Sea Marine Park.
L195: ## Video
L196: 
L197: Using remote sensing technologies and an underwater drone, scientists from Schmidt Ocean Institute made some amazing discoveries while uncovering the depths of the Coral Sea Marine Park during the Visioning Coral Sea expedition. Watch more videos on cite119†YouTube†www.youtube.com .

L215: cite123†Download map L216: ## Explore
L217: 
L218: For those who make the journey, this marine park rewards visitors with exceptional diving, boating, snorkelling, nature watching and fishing.
L219: 
L220: Most people visiting the marine park travel on live-aboard tour boats from Port Douglas, Cairns, Townsville, Mackay, Airlie Beach or Gladstone, often calling in at some Great Barrier Reef sites on the way.
L221: The cite124†Be Pest Free in the Coral Sea biosecurity information sheet provides information to people visiting the Coral Sea Marine Park about the importance of stopping pests such as ants and rodents from being introduced onto islands. If you visit the remote islands in the Coral Sea Marine Park you need to consider your impact and ways to protect the seabirds, turtles and plants that make up these amazing but vulnerable island ecosystems.
L222: For divers, some of the most prized underwater sites are in the Coral Sea Marine Park. Explore the cite125†reefs of the Coral Sea , including Holmes Reef and Bougainville Reef, each with unique features and a rich variety of species to enjoy.
L223: 
L224: The wild and remote cite126†Osprey Reef has been listed as one of the top ten dive sites in the world.
L225: 
L226: Some of the locals you may encounter include:
L227:   * cite127†whales and dolphins L228:   * cite128†turtles L229:   * cite129†seabirds L230:   * cite130†giant hunters like marlin, swordfish, tuna and sharks L231: 
L232: You might even spot a humpback whale between June and November.
L233: 
L234: There are at least 45 historic shipwrecks in the Coral Sea Marine Park. Find out more about the cite131†military and maritime history in the Coral Sea.
L235: 
L236: Fishing in the pristine waters of the Coral Sea is a once-in-a-lifetime experience. You could expect to encounter:
L237:   * marlin, both black and blue
L238:   * dogtooth tuna
L239:   * giant trevally
L240:   * mahi mahi
L241:   * wahoo
L242:   * many other species.
L243: 
L244: Most charter fishing trips will take you on three day or more live-aboard voyages to experience some amazing fishing on isolated reef systems.
L245: 
L246: The park also supports commercial fishing and shipping, which contribute to economic growth, employment and social wellbeing in Queensland coastal towns and communities.
L247: Recreational fishing is allowed in much of the Coral Sea Marine Park, but not in the National Park zones. Check which zone you’re in before you start to fish.
L248: 
L249: Explore more of the Coral Sea:
L250: 
L251:   * cite132†The Coral Sea - an overview L252:   * cite133†Under the Coral Sea L253: ## Discover
L254: 
L255: The Coral Sea Marine Park is an ecologically significant place and an amazing destination.
L256: 
L257: Problems such as marine pollution, illegal fishing, climate change and invasive species can impact marine environments around the world, including remote ones like the Coral Sea.
L258: 
L259: Parks Australia is looking after the Coral Sea Marine Park by working in partnership with:
L260: 
L261:   * communities
L262:   * scientists
L263:   * other government departments
L264:   * New Caledonia.
L265: ## New Caledonia
L266: 
L267: Our intention to work collaboratively with New Caledonia was formalised in 2010, through a joint declaration that sets out our desire to work together on science, management and regional capacity building activities.
L268: 
L269: The progress of activities under the Declaration is periodically published in a newsletter. They are available in both English and French. This work is helping us learn more about the Coral Sea Marine Park, and find the best ways to protect it now and into the future.

L282:   * cite141†Coral Sea Natural Park New Caledonia [PDF, 2 MB] L283: ## Marine debris
L284: 
L285: Marine debris (rubbish in the oceans) is a global problem.
L286: 
L287: Debris includes:
L288: 
L289:   * discarded and lost fishing nets and buoys
L290:   * millions of plastic bags
L291:   * water bottles
L292:   * countless tiny bits of plastic (microplastics).
L293: 
L294: Some rubbish is dumped directly into the oceans. Other pieces are lost at sea. A lot starts on land, travelling to the oceans in drains and waterways, or on the wind.
L295: 
L296: Marine debris kills marine life through entanglement and ingestion:
L297:   * Turtles and birds get tangled in discarded nets and drown.
L298:   * Seabirds eat plastic, thinking it is food, and their chicks starve when fed regurgitated plastic instead of fish.
L299: 
L300: Microplastics and their compounds make their way up the food chain, including into the seafood we eat.
L301: 
L302: And marine debris spoils the places we like to visit, making beaches unsightly.

L16: ### We want people to 'see the Reef, love the Reef, protect the Reef'.

L20: cite6†We are the Reef Authority | Managing and protecting the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park†www.youtube.com L21: ## The Reef: vast, beautiful and under pressure
L22: 
L23: The Great Barrier Reef is a global icon and an integral part of Australia’s national identity. The Great Barrier Reef is a vast and spectacular ecosystem and one of the most complex natural systems on Earth.
L24: This World Heritage Area with Outstanding Universal Value is an economic powerhouse, contributing $9 billion to Australia’s national economy as well as some 77,000 jobs. Unsurprisingly, tourism remains the Reef’s largest contributor to economic activity, with around $7.9 billion in value added to the Australian economy due to the Reef. The Great Barrier Reef is valued at $95 billion.
L25: As the world’s largest coral reef ecosystem, it is bigger in size than Italy, and spans 2300 kilometres of Australia’s north-east coast. It comprises almost 3000 individual reefs, about 10 per cent of the world’s coral reefs.
L26: 
L27: However, the Great Barrier Reef, like all coral reefs globally is under pressure and actions taken now will matter.
L28: ## Health and threats to the Reef
L29: 
L30: The Great Barrier Reef remains a vast and spectacular ecosystem, but its integrity is being increasingly challenged by cumulative pressures, predominately from climate change.
L31: 
L32: The cite7†Great Barrier Reef Outlook Report 2024 highlights that strong and effective actions are urgent at global, regional and local scales.
L33: As identified in the Report, the greatest threat to the Reef is climate change. The other main threats are associated with land-based run-off, coastal development,  and threats from direct human use of the Reef (such as illegal fishing).
L34: Our cite8†position statements on cite9†climate change†hdl.handle.net , cite10†fishing†elibrary.gbrmpa.gov.au , cite11†coastal ecosystems†elibrary.gbrmpa.gov.au , cite12†water quality†elibrary.gbrmpa.gov.au and cite13†marine debris†elibrary.gbrmpa.gov.au encourage immediate, medium and long-term action for threats to the Reef.
L35: ## Securing the Reef's future
L36: 
L37: The Reef remains one of the best-managed marine ecosystems in the world and science is central to our cite1†management†hdl.handle.net .
L38: 
L39: The Great Barrier Reef received World Heritage status in 1981, the first coral reef ecosystem in the world to have this distinction. It was inscribed by the World Heritage Committee for its ‘outstanding universal value’.
L40: The Australian and Queensland governments’ cite14†Reef 2050 Long‑Term Sustainability Plan†www.environment.gov.au provides a guiding framework for securing the future of the Great Barrier Reef. It outlines key management actions being taken to reduce threats to the Reef. Underpinning the Reef 2050 Plan, is the development of a world class monitoring and reporting system to inform adaptive management.
L41: The cite15†Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Zoning Plan 2003  and related legislation are the foundation of our resilience-based management approach.
L42: 
L43: cite16†Zoning to protect biodiversity and regulate activities has been in place since 1981. Since 2004, some 33 per cent of the entire Marine Park is in highly protected zones.
L44: 
L45: Plans of management and our permissions system provide for ecologically-sustainable multiple-use of the Reef.
L46: Collaborative management through programs, like the cite17†Reef Joint Field Management Program with the cite18†Queensland Parks and Wildlife Service†parks.des.qld.gov.au , are critical to the Reef’s future.
L47: ## Partnerships
L48: 
L49: Establishing effective and meaningful partnerships with cite19†Traditional Owners is essential to protect cultural and heritage values, conserve biodiversity and enhance the resilience of the Great Barrier Reef.
L50: 
L51: We are working in partnership with Traditional Owner groups to develop Sea Country management arrangements including cite20†Traditional Use of Marine Resources Agreements , which are co-designed and co-managed by the Traditional Owners, the Authority and the Queensland Government.
L52: The cite21†Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Heritage Strategy for the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park†hdl.handle.net outlines how we will work with Traditional Owners to help keep the Indigenous heritage values of the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park strong, safe and healthy.
L53: 
L54: The strategy is a significant step in honouring the knowledge and value of cite22†Traditional Owner connections to the Reef and sets a path for greater co-management of the Reef.
L55: The Great Barrier Reef tourism industry, including through the cite23†Master Reef Guides program , plays a vital role in presenting the values of the World Heritage Area to millions of visitors annually.
L56: Through targeted education and stewardship programs, including our national educational centre cite24†Great Barrier Reef Aquarium†www.greatbarrierreefaquarium.au (currently closed for redevelopment), we ensure the community and stakeholders have a clear understanding of the value of the Great Barrier Reef, the threats to its sustainable future and their role in protecting it.
L57: Our cite25†Reef Guardian program and cite26†Local Marine Advisory Committees help facilitate education programs with schools, and actions with regional councils and fishers, and the community to help protect the Reef.
L58: Global collaboration is imperative for the health of the Reef. We are committed to sharing our expertise and success stories and promoting leading practice coral reef management with our international partners, including through the cite27†International Coral Reef Initiative , an informal partnership between nations and organisations that strives to preserve coral reefs and associated ecosystems around the world.
L59: ## Actions taken now will matter
L60: 
L61: Given the extensive size of the Great Barrier Reef Region, its condition is variable. Many areas continue to support beautiful corals and abundant marine life and the Reef remains an extraordinary experience for visitors.
L62: 
L63: The Reef has shown the ability to recover from impacts, if disturbance-free periods are long-enough.
L64: Mitigating threats like climate change and poor water quality, coupled with resilience-based management, are essential to boosting Reef health so it can recover from major disturbances.
L65: 
L66: Sea temperature increase and extremes, such as marine heat waves, are the most immediate threats to the Reef as a whole and pose the highest risk. The strongest and fastest possible global action on climate change is critical, and everyone can contribute and make a difference.
L67: While the challenge is big, it is achievable. As acknowledged in the cite28†Great Barrier Reef Blueprint for Climate Resilience and Adaptation .
L68: 
L69: ‘Together we can secure the future of the Great Barrier Reef, but we need to try harder, do more, and act now’.

L96: Geological values
L97: 
L98: The geology of the Great Barrier Reef tells the story of its earliest origins and today reveals the foundations it is built upon. The earliest Great Barrier Reef origins are held deep in its geology, telling the story of drifting continents as the foundations for its existence.
L99: 
L100: The first organism to accumulate limestone existed long before animals, including corals, evolved. About 3.7 billion years ago, blue-green algae formed stony mounts and columns.
L101: Some 1500 million years later, primitive sponge-like creatures became the next animals to produce limestone structures.
L102: 
L103: Around 25 million years ago, As Australia continued to drift northwards into the tropics, small coral reefs had formed far offshore, and a few reefs on the edge of Australia's continental shelf had also established in the very far north.
L104: 
L105: Approximately half a million years ago, the northernmost part of the Great Barrier began to form and is now the oldest part of the Great Barrier Reef.
L106: Throughout its half-million-year history, the Great Barrier Reef has gone through several ice ages, called glacial periods, during which sea levels drop. These times alternated with warmer periods, called interglacial periods, where sea levels rise again.
L107: 
L108: These cycles are caused by a wobble in the Earth's rotational axis that alters the amount of sunlight reaching parts of the planet.

L145: Biodiversity values
L146: ### What is biodiversity?
L147: 
L148: Biodiversity is the variety among living things, and the Great Barrier Reef's biodiversity forms part of the basis of its outstanding universal value recognised in its world heritage listing.
L149: 
L150: Biodiversity includes all-natural variation, from genetic differences within a species to variations across a habitat or a whole ecosystem.
L151: The Great Barrier Reef is one of the world's most diverse and remarkable ecosystems, with a range of habitats and many thousands of different species.
L152: 
L153: Every species, in its effort to survive long enough to reproduce, affects the ecosystem in a particular way. In attempting to understand how ecosystems work, scientists describe these effects as 'services' such as decomposing waste or grazing away algae that keep the ecosystem functioning.
L154: ### Why is biodiversity so important?
L155: 
L156: Biodiversity is not just nice; it is necessary. Nothing can survive in isolation. Even some of the basic ecosystem services include the maintenance of water, air and soil quality - factors important for much of the life on Earth.
L157: 
L158: If services stopped, an ecosystem could collapse to a different state, with the loss of many species.
L159: 
L160: Biodiversity is the source of all of our foods, and many of our medicines and industrial products are derived from animals and plants.
L161: Biodiversity is important for our recreation and our physical and spiritual well-being.
L162: 
L163: It is the reason people travel to visit the Great Barrier Reef, to see life in abundance. A diverse environment has a profound aesthetic appeal to all human beings.
L164: Reef ecology - Food webs: All reef plants and animals are part of an intricate, functional and interconnected food web. Impact on any population has flow-on effects on other reef species. Depending on their functional ecosystem role, the loss of a species population can have enormous consequences.
L165: 
L166: Basic ecological roles include Primary Producers, First Order Consumers, Second Order Consumers, Scavengers and Decomposers.
L167: Reef ecology -  Beyond food webs: Understanding that the Great Barrier Reef ecosystem is a giant food web, there is a range of related processes to understand to help share how the system works.
L168: 
L169: Some critical examples of these processes include the Zooxanthellae symbiotic relationship with coral and other animals, the fact that bacteria are everywhere, nutrients are quickly recycled and connectivity is a fundamental driver of Reef health.

L217: 
L218: Components include other lightstations,  shipwrecks, aircraft wrecks  and other places of historic  significance. Published condition  and trend data are lacking for most  sites, so confidence in the grade  and trend is limited or inferred.
L219: 
L220: Positive progress has been made  towards gathering evidence on  shipwrecks and aircraft wrecks.
L221: The significant discovery in late 2018 of the precise location of the shipwreck of the Martha Ridgway increased the baseline data for this component.
L222: 
L223: The vessel was lost over 170 years ago on a voyage from New Zealand to Bombay (now Mumbai).
L224: The Martha Ridgway shipwreck was found on the reef of the same name using a variety of survey methods and remote sensing equipment,  including aerial surveys (drone), magnetometer surveys and visual census. The wreck is significant for many reasons, including its size and its association with the historic Raine Island beacon.
L225: Other heritage values: Social, aesthetic and scientific values are included in this assessment. The significance of the World Heritage Area still transcends national boundaries and remains a source of pride for the Australian public broadly.
L226: 
L227: The social heritage value of the Region is considered to be in good condition. How society thinks and feels about the state of the Reef is at the heart of the Region‘s social heritage value.
L228: In 2017, climate change, pollution and agricultural run-off were considered by Australian residents to be the biggest threats to the Reef.
L229: 
L230: A 2017 survey of approximately 3900 people living close to or deriving benefit from the Reef (local and national residents,  tourists, tourism operators, and commercial fishers) highlighted the wider community’s concern about the declining condition of the Reef, and a strengthening connection to its environment and natural beauty.

L19: 
L20: Plunge into the clear, warm waters for an amazing snorkel experience just metres from shore, venture to some deeper water to swim with whale sharks, or just relax on the beach and pick up that book you’ve been meaning to read.
L21: 
L22: Ningaloo Marine Park is World Heritage-listed and one of the largest fringing reefs home to hundreds of fish and coral species, making snorkelling as easy as a short paddle from shore.
L23: There’s more than just fish to see, organise a guided experience with whale sharks, humpback whales, manta rays, turtles, dolphins or dugongs! If you’d rather stay dry, get a glimpse of the reef via a glass bottom boat tour.
L24: The best time to catch the whale sharks on their migration is between March and August and the humpbacks are hanging out from June to November. If you’re around during the warmer months of February and March you can watch turtle hatchlings make their first dash to the sea and join an eco-education tour at Jurabi Turtle Centre.
L25: Cast a line from the beach, your own boat or a charter tour. The reef is home to a heap of sport and game fish, just make sure to follow the rules and avoid sanctuary areas. Catch a wave in Exmouth with surf lessons and boards for hire, or for some more serious surf head towards Carnarvon to Gnarloo, Red Bluff and Quobba Stations.

L108: ## Commonwealth waters
L109: 
L110: The cite28†Commonwealth Ningaloo Marine Park†parksaustralia.gov.au borders the western edge of the State Ningaloo Marine Park. It incorporates a diversity of habitats including the continental slope and shelf, as well as pelagic habitats in the open ocean.
L111: 
L112: The deeper waters are dominated by sponge gardens with soft corals and algae. The open ocean supports large numbers of fish such as trevally, tuna, mackerel, marlin and sailfish.
L113: Humpback whales pass through twice a year on their annual migration. Blue, sperm, minke, Bryde’s, southern right and killer whales have all been observed in the Commonwealth waters, while whale sharks and dolphins are frequent visitors.
